title: Fair and Explainable Credit-Scoring under Concept Drift: Adaptive Explanation Frameworks for Evolving Populations
tldr: Adaptive SHAP-based explanation frameworks improve temporal stability and fairness in credit-scoring systems under concept drift without degrading predictive accuracy.
problem_and_motivation: Explainable AI techniques like SHAP assume static data distributions, making their explanations unstable and potentially unfair when concept drift occurs in credit-scoring systems. This creates challenges for regulatory compliance and trust as borrower behaviors and economic conditions evolve over time.
approach: Multi-year lending dataset spanning 2015-2024 with demographic, financial, and socioeconomic features.
XGBoost baseline model with time-aware expanding-window validation strategy.
Three adaptive SHAP variants: per-slice reweighting, sliding-window rebaselining, and online surrogate calibration.
Drift detection using PSI, KS test, JS divergence, and Chi-square tests.
Fairness auditing across demographic attributes using DPD, EOD, and EODs metrics.
Evaluation of explanation stability using cosine similarity, Kendall tau, and Jaccard overlap.
findings: num: AUC values ranged from 0.63-0.66 across test years despite drift.
num: Adaptive methods achieved cosine similarity of approximately 0.995 and Kendall tau of 0.89.
num: Method B reduced demographic parity difference by approximately 0.026 (p < 0.05).
num: Default rates increased from approximately 15% in 2015 to over 23% in 2024.
num: PSI for annual_income reached approximately 0.16 by 2019.
num: Top features by final year SHAP values were loan_amount (0.055), dti (0.034), credit_score (0.023).
Adaptive methods preserved semantic continuity in explanations across evolving data.
Proxy variable detection identified loan_amount, credit_score, and annual_income as statistically associated with race.
key_figures_tables: Figure 1: Loan default rate by year → Default rates increased from 15% to 23% over decade.
Figure 4: Model test AUC over test years → AUC remained stable between 0.63-0.66.
Figure 7: DPD before and after method B recalibration → Fairness disparities declined markedly.
Figure 10: Kendall tau and Cosine similarity over test years → Adaptive methods showed consistent improvements.
Figure 12: Number of harmful features detected by explainability methods → Adaptive methods reduced proxy variable prominence.

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: This paper advances the field of explainable AI in financial systems by addressing the critical gap between static explainability tools and dynamic data environments. It introduces three adaptive SHAP-based methods that maintain interpretive stability under concept drift, demonstrating that explanation frameworks can evolve alongside data. The research contributes longitudinal evaluation methodologies for tracking fairness and explanation drift over multi-year periods. It establishes that adaptive recalibration can reduce demographic parity differences without compromising predictive performance, providing practical mechanisms for responsible AI in credit-scoring.
directly_justifies: Adaptive SHAP variants substantially improve temporal stability and reduce disparate impact across demographic groups.
Method B achieves highest cosine and Kendall stability scores year-over-year through sliding-window background sampling.
Adaptive methods preserve semantic continuity in explanations across evolving data landscapes.
Fairness disparities declined markedly after applying group recalibration mechanism embedded in Method B.
limits: Study focuses mainly on single-attribute fairness rather than overlapping demographic factors.
SHAP analysis can be computationally heavy, especially when applied repeatedly across large datasets.
Financial dataset used may not fully capture real-world challenges like missing information or regulatory limits.
topic_relevance.topic_mapping_rationale: Systematic scan across all 14 topic domains identified high relevance in domains 5 (Financial Behavioral Profiles), 6 (Predictive Modeling), 8 (Anomaly Detection), and 12 (Evaluation Frameworks). Domain 5.A is relevant as the paper analyzes evolving borrower behavioral profiles. Domain 6.A applies through XGBoost predictive modeling with expanding-window validation. Domain 8.A is relevant for concept drift detection as a distributional anomaly. Domain 12.A applies through the comprehensive evaluation framework for explanation stability and fairness. Borderline cases included domain 4 (Existing Systems) due to literature review of credit-scoring systems, but marked low relevance. Domains 1-3 (demographics, cultural practices, expense categorization) and 9-11 (mobile design, privacy, engagement) were rejected as not directly addressed. Domain 13 (savings/debt management) is tangentially related but not the paper's focus. Overall, the paper primarily contributes to algorithmic fairness and explainability in financial predictive modeling.

limitations: SHAP analysis is computationally heavy, especially with repeated application across large datasets or time windows.
Fairness assessment focuses mainly on single attributes like race or gender rather than intersecting demographic factors.
Real-world financial data brings additional challenges like missing information, delayed updates, and regulatory limits not fully captured.
Study uses simulated economic conditions rather than actual banking data.
remember_this: Adaptive SHAP methods improve explanation stability under concept drift without sacrificing accuracy.
Method B (sliding-window rebaselining) delivered most consistent improvements in temporal stability.
Fairness disparities reduced by approximately 0.026 after adaptive recalibration (p < 0.05).
Explanation frameworks can evolve alongside data to maintain transparency and accountability.
Adaptive explainability supports responsible AI in credit-scoring systems.
